brief: Ahead of the Treasury's first expanded buyback, BofA's Mark Cabana expected a purchase near the $6 billion maximum, reasoning that 10y-20y operations had averaged $18.7 billion of offers, about 9 times oversubscribed against the old $2 billion cap, and that Treasury had always bought the maximum, so a sub-max purchase would be unprecedented. A competing game-theoretical view held that the more Treasury bought, the stronger the distress signal, sparking a further selloff with yields already at 3-year highs. The operation drew $10.5 billion of offers and Treasury accepted just under half, $5.187 billion, below the $6 billion cap and only the third sub-max result in 53 operations since 2024. A quarter of accepted offers were lowballs. Yields rose, with the 10-year up 10 basis points to 4.94%. Cabana argues that if the back-end selloff is not contained, Treasury may cut long-end auction sizes or eliminate the 20-year bond. Strategists estimate coupon cuts like 2021-2022 carry about 20 basis points of rate impact and eliminating the 20- and 30-year as much as 53. BofA still recommends buying the dip on 30-year spreads while warning of more pain first.
